rv.q: This, Lyndsey Turner's gripping revival at the National magnificently manages to do.
A great play has found a powerful, timely production.
It's an unforgettable opening to Lyndsey Turner's magnificent revival of The Crucible, setting up the chilling horror in which humanity turns in on itself with deadly consequences.
Director Lyndsey Turner makes the three hours of morality flawed – and floored – by madness fly by.
It's another masterly touch in a production that hardly puts a foot wrong.
Turner's vision of The Crucible is bleak but hugely rewarding, digging deep into the violent paranoia and creating a convincing blood lust dressed up as justice that grips Salem.
In serving Miller's text with discipline and care, Turner's staging is both sturdy and elegant, allowing contrary impulses to clash with shattering results.
It is a scene that draws especially fine performances from Rachelle Diedericks as Mary, Karl Johnson as Giles and Brendan Cowell as Proctor.
Part of the trouble with this new revival is that it lacks a clear perspective because the attention-grabbing production swamps the play.

cn.t: A visually slick production that generates terror only intermittently, elevated by strong supporting performances but ultimately fails to fully realize the source material's potential.
